question: What does Gita Gopinath mean by 'the great gamble'?
gold_answer: She means the world is betting on two big forces pulling in opposite directions: AI and geopolitics. Countries in the AI super cycle benefit, while those hit by tariffs and conflict lose, and so far it has been a wash. It is a gamble because these are very big policy decisions, such as moving away from the rules-based trading system with agreed tariff rules and the WTO, at a time when the world has never been more integrated.
key_points: two forces: AI and geopolitics; AI positive, tariffs and conflict negative, so far a wash; moving away from rules-based trading system; world more integrated than ever

question: Is there a simple exercise Vinh Giang recommends to get better at listening?
gold_answer: Yes, a game called 'last word, last letter': while planning something together (he uses planning a lunch), each person must start their sentence with the last letter of the other person's last word. It shows how hard it is to listen, and it teaches the behaviour of a great listener: not thinking about a reply while the other person talks, letting them finish, pausing, then responding.
key_points: game called last word, last letter; start your sentence with the last letter of the other person's last word; great listener does not plan a reply while the other talks; let them finish, pause, then respond

question: Which business opportunity does Sachin Puri think people are sleeping on?
gold_answer: Elder care. He says the world's population is ageing: about 11 to 12% of India's population is already over 60 and it will be more than 20% by 2050 (roughly 350 million people, about the population of the US). India lacks an established ecosystem for social security and care facilities, there is stigma around nursing homes, families are moving from joint to nuclear, and the sector is highly unorganised and purely SMB, so providing safe, predictable care for elders is one of the biggest opportunities.

question: How does Gamma judge whether a new model or prompt is better, when evals can't measure taste?
gold_answer: The Gamma co-founder says evals are hard for subjective, taste-oriented questions such as 'does this look cool' or 'is this me'. They use some proxy evals for objective things (does it follow instructions, does it stick to the brand guideline), but because their user base is so diverse they rely much more on A/B testing: running two models or two prompts at large scale and measuring which performs better across users, which captures subjectivity. He adds that founders compete by bringing taste to their domain.
key_points: evals hard for taste; proxy evals like instruction following and brand guidelines; rely on A/B testing two models or prompts at scale; founders bring taste
author: pm_proxy

question: I'm a PM at an established company launching a second product. Does Rob Snyder's approach still apply to us?
gold_answer: Yes. He is helping companies launch second products by 'running it back': founders take the same approach to existing customers, selling new features before they are built in order to upsell. A product leader told him every idea that worked came from sales calls where customers asked 'could you also do this other thing for us?', and the whiteboarded ones never worked. So put up a hypothesis, talk to five existing customers, look for pull and whether they will actually buy. Ideally founders do this selling; if you are a non-founder doing zero to one, focus on selling and learning through selling.
key_points: same approach with existing customers; sell new features before building; ideas from sales calls worked, whiteboarded ones did not; test with five existing customers; non-founders should learn through selling
author: pm_proxy

question: Should I pitch my product to enterprise buyers as the cheaper option? What does Jen Abel say?
gold_answer: It depends which of two motions you are in. One is 'I need the lowest-cost way to do X' for something low on the totem pole, where 60% of the way there is fine and the buyer just wants to save budget. The other is solving a high-risk problem that lets you charge a $250K to $500K land; legal, for example, needs to stomp out risk (missing information, delays, new regulation). The more you sell alpha and upside rather than cost savings, the more you can charge.
key_points: two motions: lowest-cost for low-priority problems vs high-risk problems; high-risk lets you charge 250-500K land; legal is about stomping out risk; alpha and upside let you charge more
author: pm_proxy

question: Should I design the product before letting an AI agent write the code?
gold_answer: Yes. Nick's process is research first, then design everything in Paper (via its MCP) before building anything, iterating on variations (diverge, then converge). In the Ross Mike episode, Greg says the mistake people make is going straight to code, which produces 'AI smell' slop; take a moment to make sure the design system is high quality and fits the ICP first. Ross agrees: he locks the design in Paper, uses comments as feedback, then has it generate code, because changing a deployed site means rebuilding.
key_points: research then design in Paper before building; don't go straight to code (AI smell); lock the design system first, then generate code
author: pm_proxy

question: Is it worth running a pilot with an enterprise prospect before they sign?
gold_answer: The guests differ. Jen Abel treats the pilot as a step in the process: keep it short and time-boxed (two to three days, not two weeks), put the real users in it (not the C-level), and she would rather forgo charging so she can control the sales cycle, though you should charge if they need a month or integration with their data. About 80% should succeed after the pilot. Rob Snyder recommends no pilots, proofs of concept or design partners: go straight to selling and rolling it out, and only pilot if the buyer says that is how they buy, never offering it proactively.
key_points: Jen: short time-boxed pilot of 2-3 days with real users; charge only if long or needs integration; about 80% succeed post-pilot; Rob: no pilots or POCs, don't offer proactively, only if the buyer requires it
